**The Baseus Blade H1 (20,000 mAh, 100 W) is a good pick for flying.** The search results only covered this one product, so I can't say it beats every alternative. It fits the airline rules, and it can charge a laptop and a phone.

**Why it works for a plane**
- It's about 74 Wh, under the 100 Wh limit for power banks ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)).
- It has 100 W USB-C output, 2 USB-C and 2 USB-A ports, and pass-through charging.
- It's flat (134 × 134 × 18 mm, about 451 g), so it fits in a personal item.
- It costs $89.99 (list $99.99), checked on 2026-10-21, with a 24-month warranty and a 7-day return window ([Dealectric listing](https://dealectric.com/baseus-blade-h1-100w-20000mah)).
- Caveat: Baseus doesn't publish per-port wattage or how power splits across several devices.

**Rules for any power bank on a plane**
- **Carry-on only.** Power banks can't go in checked bags. If your carry-on is gate-checked, take the power bank out and keep it with you ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7)).
- **100 Wh limit.** Larger batteries (101–160 Wh) need airline approval, and anything over 160 Wh is banned. To calculate Wh, multiply volts by amp-hours.
- **Protect the terminals.** Keep it in its retail packaging, a pouch, or a case, or tape over the terminals.
- **Don't bring a damaged or recalled battery.**
- **Check your airline's limits.** Many are stricter than the FAA. Southwest, for example, limits each customer to one power bank as of April 20, 2026. It can't be used in the overhead bin or charged from in-seat power, and it must be visible while in use ([Southwest](https://support.southwest.com/helpcenter/article/Traveling-with-lithium-batteries-e-cigarettes-and-lighters)).

If you're comparing other models, look for a printed Wh rating of 100 or less, which works out to roughly 27,000 mAh or less.
